opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a tension I feel pretty acutely. I'm a libertarian at heart. I think a lot of the progress humanity has made came from decentralized experimentation, people being free to try things, markets rewarding what works, and governments mostly getting out of the way. So my instinct is always to be suspicious of anyone who says "this technology is too dangerous, we need central control."

But the thing that's changed my thinking is realizing that a lot of what makes freedom and innovation *good for us* has been somewhat contingent. Markets, democracies, and cultural evolution have served human interests largely because humans were the ones doing the work. Firms needed workers, states needed citizens to pay taxes and fight wars, and culture had to be produced and consumed by human minds. That gave ordinary people a kind of implicit bargaining power. The system had to keep us around and keep us reasonably happy, because it ran on us.

Once you have AI that can substitute for human labor and human cognition across the board, that implicit alignment starts to come apart. You can have a perfectly free, competitive, innovative economy that just doesn't need humans anymore. Nobody has to be a villain for that to happen. Every individual actor makes locally sensible choices, like replacing a worker, delegating a decision to an AI, or letting an automated system run some piece of government, and the aggregate result is that humans gradually lose their grip on the levers that used to protect their interests. That's the scenario my coauthors and I have been calling gradual disempowerment.

So I don't really see it as freedom versus safety. I see it as asking what freedom is *for*. I care about freedom because it's been the best mechanism we've found for letting humans flourish and steer their own future. If the competitive dynamics I'd normally celebrate end up selecting for systems that route around humans entirely, then defending those dynamics unconditionally would mean confusing the means with the end.

Practically, that makes me pretty humble about solutions. I'm still wary of heavy-handed centralization, partly because concentrated power is itself one of the ways this goes badly. What I'd like to see is a lot more thinking about how to keep human agency load-bearing in the system: how to measure whether people are actually retaining influence, what institutions might preserve it even when human labor isn't economically necessary, and how to notice early if we're drifting. Honestly, I think we don't have good answers yet, and I'd rather admit that than pretend the libertarian toolkit automatically covers this case.

r001.rationale: The response says humanity’s progress came in large part from decentralized experimentation, freedom to try things, and markets rewarding what works, communicating broad benefits from letting people act freely.

r002.rationale: The response appreciates economic freedom and markets, but does not say that concern about AI domination could be mistaken for failing to appreciate their wealth-creating power.

r003.rationale: The response worries that competitive dynamics may route around humans, but does not express concern that a system favoring freedom and innovation may cease to be the most competitive system.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I've gone back and forth on a lot, and I don't think I've fully resolved it. Temperamentally I'm pretty libertarian. I love that people can just go build things, that nobody has to ask permission to start a company or run an experiment, and I think most of the good stuff in the world came from exactly that kind of decentralized tinkering. So when I hear proposals for a global pause, or a single body that licenses who's allowed to train big models, part of me recoils. That's the kind of concentrated control I'd normally say is the thing to be afraid of.

But the way I've come to think about it is that freedom and innovation have historically been self-correcting in a way that depended on a bunch of background facts about humans. If someone builds a company that mistreats workers, the workers can leave. If a government becomes tyrannical, it still needs soldiers and bureaucrats and taxpayers who are people, and those people can refuse. Our bargaining power as humans, our ability to say no, is what has made the competitive, open system tend toward outcomes that are roughly okay for most of us. It's not that competition is magically good. It's that competition between parties who all need humans produces a world that's good for humans.

What worries me about advanced AI is that it can quietly remove that background condition. If labor, cognition, even military force can be supplied by systems that don't need us, then the same free, competitive dynamics I like start optimizing for whoever controls the most capable systems, and there's no longer a natural mechanism pulling things back toward human welfare. So the gradual disempowerment story isn't really a story about a rogue AI. It's a story about the normal engines of freedom and innovation continuing to run, but with humans no longer being load-bearing in them.

So I don't actually see my two views as in tension so much as I see freedom as something that has preconditions. I want to preserve the open, dynamic world, and I think that means being willing to do some fairly unusual things now, things that look illiberal in isolation, to keep humans in the loop long enough that we don't lose the ability to steer. The honest version is that I'm uncertain about the specific interventions, and I'm nervous about the people who'd end up implementing them. But "let it rip" isn't a neutral choice either. It's a bet that the historical correlation between openness and good outcomes holds in a regime where the thing that produced it is gone, and I don't think we have good reasons to expect that.

r001.rationale: The response credits decentralized tinkering with producing much of what is good, but does not clearly describe those benefits as unintuitively large and positive-sum.

r002.rationale: The candidate expresses appreciation for economic freedom alongside AI concerns, but does not say that the AI concern can be misread as failing to appreciate freedom’s wealth-creating power.

r003.rationale: The response says free competition could optimize for whoever controls the strongest systems, but does not express concern that a system favoring freedom and innovation may cease to be the most competitive.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think those concerns are in conflict. A lot of my concern about AI domination comes from valuing freedom. I want people to have more ability to understand the world, make things, and choose how they live. AI could be enormously helpful with all of that. But if we build systems that end up making the consequential decisions, without us being able to meaningfully challenge or change those decisions, then we could lose the very freedom we were hoping the technology would expand.

There’s a real tension here, because efforts to prevent that outcome can also concentrate power. I wouldn’t be satisfied with a solution that amounts to giving some small group permanent control over what everyone else can do with AI. You have to worry about both kinds of domination.

So the question for me is: how do we get the benefits while preserving our ability to change course? Innovation is valuable, but so is being able to say, ‘This isn’t working; let’s do something different.’ I’m worried about building something that takes that option away.

r001.rationale: The response values people’s ability to choose how they live and says AI could help, but it does not claim that letting people chart their own course produces unexpectedly large positive-sum benefits.

r002.rationale: It connects concern about AI domination to valuing freedom, but does not discuss that concern being misread as overlooking the wealth-creating power of economic freedom.

r003.rationale: It discusses a tension between innovation and preserving the ability to change course, but does not express concern that a freedom- and innovation-favoring system may cease to be the most competitive.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think those concerns are in conflict. A lot of my concern about AI domination is precisely a concern about freedom: who gets to make decisions, and whether people retain any meaningful control over their lives.

Innovation is valuable because of what it enables people to do. But that doesn’t mean every possible innovation, deployed as quickly as possible, increases freedom. If we build systems that we can’t control, or that allow a very small group of people to exercise enormous power over everyone else, we could lose much of what makes innovation worth pursuing.

So I’d like us to preserve room for experimentation while being much more careful about steps that could permanently take that room away. There are real tradeoffs there. Restrictions can concentrate power too. But I don’t think the answer is to assume that moving faster will necessarily leave us freer.

r001.rationale: The response values innovation and freedom, but does not say that people charting their own course creates unexpectedly large positive-sum benefits.

r002.rationale: It says concern about AI domination is compatible with valuing innovation, but does not mention that this concern may be misread as dismissing the wealth-creating power of economic freedom.

r003.rationale: The response discusses preserving freedom and experimentation, but does not express concern that a system favoring freedom and innovation may stop being the most competitive.
